newsitem.title: INDIA: Activists told forget Miss World, help prostitutes.
newsitem.headline: Activists told forget Miss World, help prostitutes.

text.p: Protesters against the Miss World pageant in India should redirect their energies against a cult sentencing thousands of young girls to a life of prostitution, the Indian Health Organisation (IHO) said on Monday.
Dr. I.S. Gilada, secretary-general of the independently funded IHO, accused activists of picking on Miss World because it would grab media attention rather than a bigger issue closer to home.
Members of a militant traditionalist women's group have threatened to commit suicide by burning themselves to death unless the beauty show is halted.
Local members of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, and left-wing groups have also joined the anti-Miss World camp.
The protesters say the show demeans women, corrupts Indian culture, and provides further inroads for multinational companies into India.
Gilada said they were more intent on scoring political points than genuinely caring about the welfare of women.
"It is totally political. They know the media will follow Miss World. It is a political stunt," he told Reuters.
Many women forced into religious service for the Hindu goddess Yellama, who has a large following among low caste Hindus, end up in Bombay's infamous brothels and those in nearby Pune, Gilada said.

Under a system called "Devadasi" they are wedded to the goddess, making them ineligible to marry. As a result, many families who are unable to support their daughters or find them husbands, sell them to pimps and sex traffickers.
The next Devadasi initiation ceremony will take place on the full moon in January in Saundatti, Karnataka.
Gilada estimated that up to 14,000 of the prostitutes in Bombay and up to 10,000 in Pune were victims of the Devadasi system.
Virtually all the girls ordered into Devadasi become prostitutes, he said. Some five percent end up either back in the safety of their better off families or begging.
Gilada also slammed the practice of nude worship of the goddess Yellama at Chandraguti, also in Karnataka, although local sources say this cult has virtually died out.
Both "nude worship" and "Devadasi" have been outlawed by the authorities but continue, and the groups campaigning against Miss World have remained silent for years, Gilada said.
"They have ignored those issues. If they really cared about the exploitation of women they should really target these first," he said.

The IHO, aside from calling on the activists to refocus their attention on these issues, also called upon the organisers of Miss World set aside money for the welfare of prostitutes and their children and to help fight against HIV and AIDS.
Prostitution is legal in India for women over 18, but forcing others to work as prostitutes is illegal.
There are thought to be more than 70,000 prostitutes working the slums of Bombay alone, where diseases including HIV and AIDS are rife.
